subject: geography
title: Feedback Loops, Mitigation and Adaptation
welcome_lead: Climate change is not linear — feedback loops can accelerate it. Explore both reducing the cause and managing the consequences.
meta_desc: Geography Adventure: positive and negative feedbacks, mitigation strategies and adaptation.
final_note: You have walked between mitigation and adaptation. Effective response requires both — with sharp attention to equity.

Process counteracting change, e.g. increased plant growth absorbing CO₂.

walkthroughs.body_html: The ice-albedo feedback: melting ice exposes darker water/land, absorbing more energy, accelerating melt. Methane release from thawing permafrost and clathrates is another concerning positive feedback. Negative feedbacks include increased outgoing longwave radiation and possible CO₂ fertilisation of plants, though these are weaker.

Decarbonisation of electricity (solar, wind, hydro, nuclear), transport (EVs, mass transit), buildings (efficiency, heat pumps) and industry (green hydrogen, electrification) underpins mitigation pathways. Nature-based solutions like afforestation and mangrove restoration store carbon. CCS and direct air capture remain expensive but feature in IPCC pathways.

Sea walls and managed retreat in the Netherlands and Bangladesh, drought-resistant crops in the Sahel, urban cooling strategies in Singapore and early warning systems in Mozambique illustrate adaptation. Climate justice requires that adaptation finance and technology transfer support vulnerable countries that contributed least to emissions.

mcqs.q: Why is the Demographic Transition Model criticised for not applying to all countries?
options: The DTM only applies to countries with more than 50 million people.
All countries follow the five stages of the DTM in order.
Primary data is collected in primary schools and secondary data in secondary schools.

It was based on European industrialisation. LICs today face different conditions: imported medicine without industrialisation, cultural factors, gender inequality and globalised economies — not all follow the same path.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between primary and secondary data in geography fieldwork?
options: Primary data is collected first-hand by the researcher (surveys, measurements, observations); secondary data already exists and is found in sources (census data, maps, published reports).
Primary data is more important and secondary data is less reliable.
Primary data is collected in primary schools and secondary data in secondary schools.
Qualitative data means high-quality data and quantitative means a lot of data.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between qualitative and quantitative data?
options: The DTM only applies to countries with more than 50 million people.
Quantitative data is numerical and measurable (traffic counts, river width); qualitative data is descriptive and non-numerical (interview quotes, photo descriptions, field sketches).
Qualitative data means high-quality data and quantitative means a lot of data.
Quantitative data is always more scientific and reliable than qualitative.
